title: Code Peer Review with GitHub
text:
Preface
Hello! :wave:

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 What is Code Peer Review? Why on Github?
Code peer review is when you look at another student’s code and give them helpful feedback, just like when you review each other’s essays. At the same time, other students will review your code and give you feedback. This helps everyone learn from each other and improve their coding skills. Learning to review code and use GitHub will help you in your career because:

title: 1  Introduction
text:
Most tech companies use GitHub or similar tools
Code review is a standard practice in professional programming
It teaches you to read and understand other people’s code
It helps you write clearer, better code
It’s a valuable skill to mention in job applications

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 What is GitHub?
GitHub is a website that programmers use to share and work on code together. Think of it like Google Docs, but specifically designed for computer code. Don’t worry if you’ve never used it before - this guide will walk you through everything step by step!

title: 2  Set-up for Teachers
text:
2.2 GitHub Setup

GitHub Organization: Create or have access to a GitHub organization for your module (e.g., UCL-StatSci-STAT0001-2025).
Personal Access Token (PAT): Create a GitHub Personal Access Token with the following permissions (scopes):

repo (full control of private repositories)
admin:org (full control of organizations and teams)
user (update user data)

title: 2  Set-up for Teachers
text:
2.3 Package Installation
Install the codeinput package from GitHub in your R console:
# Install devtools if you don't already have it
if (!requireNamespace("devtools", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("devtools")
}

# Install the codeinput package from GitHub
devtools::install_github("https://github.com/stats-ucl/code-peer-review")

title: 2  Set-up for Teachers
text:
2.4 GitHub Authentication in R
You can configure your GitHub token interactively using codeinput::run_setup() or codeinput::setup_github_token(), which supports two methods:
Option 1: gitcreds credential store (Recommended)
usethis::create_github_token(scopes = c("repo", "admin:org", "user"))
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
Option 2: Project .Renviron file
usethis::edit_r_environ(scope = "project")
# Add the line:
# GITHUB_TOKEN=your_token_here
To verify your authentication and organization access at any time, run:
library(codeinput)
test_github_connection("UCL-StatSci-STAT0001-2025")

title: 3  Overview for Teachers
text: 3.1 Quick Start with codeinput

title: 3  Overview for Teachers
text:
3.1.1 1. Installation and Initial Setup (One-Time)
First, install the codeinput package from GitHub if you haven’t already:
if (!requireNamespace("devtools", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("devtools")
}
devtools::install_github("https://github.com/stats-ucl/code-peer-review")
Next, load the package and run the interactive setup function in your project directory:
# In RStudio/R console
library(codeinput)
run_setup()
This automated setup will:

Check and install required R packages
Guide you through GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) configuration (gitcreds or .Renviron)
Create the project directory structure (submissions/, output/, output/email_templates/, output/progress_reports/, and output/reminders/)
Generate a sample student_list.csv, .gitignore, and starter scripts (main_automation_script.R and monitor_progress_script.R)
Validate your configuration with validate_configuration()



3.1.2 2. Prepare Your Data
Create your student list (student_list.csv) in the following format:
student_id,github_username,ucl_email,name
12345,alice_github,alice.smith@ucl.ac.uk,Alice Smith
12346,bob_jones,bob.jones@ucl.ac.uk,Bob Jones
12347,carol_white,carol.white@ucl.ac.uk,Carol White
To organize student submissions, download their submissions from Moodle and place them into submissions/[student_id]/ folders:
submissions/
├── 12345/
│   ├── analysis.R
│   └── data_cleaning.R
├── 12346/
│   ├── analysis.R
│   └── visualization.R


3.1.3 3. Run the Automation
Run run_automation() directly (or edit and source the generated main_automation_script.R):
library(codeinput)

results <- run_automation(
  org_name = "UCL-StatSci-STAT0001-2025",      # Your GitHub organization
  assignment_name = "assignment-1",            # Current assignment identifier
  student_list_path = "student_list.csv",      # Path to student list CSV
  submissions_path = "submissions",            # Path to student submission folders
  output_dir = "output",                       # Directory for generated output files
  reviews_per_student = 2,                     # Number of peer reviews per student
  deadline = "2025-04-15",                     # Peer review deadline
  instructor_name = "Course Instructor"        # Name for email sign-off
)
What happens automatically:

✅ Private repositories (student-{student_id}-{assignment_name}) are created for each student
✅ README.md, submission/ folder, .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/peer-review.md, and the peer-review label are set up
✅ All student submission files are uploaded to submission/
✅ Reviewer branches (reviewer-1, reviewer-2, …) are created from the uploaded submission
✅ Peer reviewers are randomly assigned in a balanced design (each student gives and receives reviews_per_student distinct reviews)
✅ Repository collaborator permissions are granted to both the submitting student and their assigned reviewers
✅ Distribution CSVs and personalized email templates are generated in output/



3.1.4 4. Distribute Access Information
All generated distribution files are saved inside the output/ directory:

output/student_repo_links.csv - Repository URLs (html_url, issues_url, pulls_url) for each student
output/reviewer_assignments.csv - Complete balanced assignment matrix (who reviews whom, including branch review URLs)
output/teacher_summary.csv - Complete overview for instructors
output/email_templates/ - Individual email_[student_id].txt files for each student and email_merge_data.csv for bulk mail merge

You can then send emails to students either by using the individual email templates or by importing output/email_templates/email_merge_data.csv into your email system for mail merge.


3.1.5 5. Monitor Progress
To track completion in real-time (or via monitor_progress_script.R), run:
library(codeinput)

report <- run_progress_check(
  org_name = "UCL-StatSci-STAT0001-2025",
  assignment_name = "assignment-1",
  student_list_path = "student_list.csv",
  output_dir = "output",
  deadline = "2025-04-15",
  instructor_name = "Course Instructor"
)
What you will get in output/:

output/progress_check_[date].csv - Repository-level progress metrics
output/student_progress_[date].csv - Student-level completion summary (reviews received)
output/reviewer_progress_[date].csv - Reviewer-level completion summary (reviews performed)
output/progress_reports/ - Visual progress plots (completion_distribution.png and issues_vs_pulls.png)
output/reminders/ - Targeted reminder emails (reminder_[reviewer_student_id].txt) for reviewers with pending reviews

The next chapter provides a detailed explanation of the workflow, customization options, and troubleshooting.

title: 4  Details for Teachers
text: 4.1 Detailed Process Walkthrough

title: 4  Details for Teachers
text:
4.1.1 GitHub Organization Setup
To create your one-time organization, follow the steps below:

Go to https://github.com/settings/organizations
Click “New organization”
Choose organization name: UCL-[Department]-[Module]-[Year]
Set to “Private” initially
Add description and contact information

The codeinput package handles all repository creation and configuration.


4.1.2 Assessment Preparation
Before running automation, prepare:
Issue Templates (automatically created):
The create_github_templates() function uploads .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/peer-review.md and creates the peer-review issue label in each student repository, providing structured sections for:

Code quality assessment
Correctness evaluation
Constructive feedback
Learning reflections

Marking Criteria Integration:
If you are using a customized fork of the package, you can edit peer_review_template in create_github_templates() (R/github_functions.R) to align with your specific marking criteria:
# Customize the peer_review_template variable in create_github_templates()
# to match your assessment goals
Assignment Instructions:
Prepare clear instructions that reference:

Learning objectives for peer review
Timeline and deadlines
Technical support resources
Assessment weighting (if applicable)



4.1.3 Student Data Collection
Collect GitHub usernames at the start of the module.
Option 1 — Moodle Survey
Create a Moodle survey with:

“GitHub username” text field

Instructions for creating GitHub accounts
Link to GitHub Education benefits

Option 2 — Submission Requirement
Include GitHub username as part of the assignment submission requirements.
Option 3 — Lab Session Collection
Collect usernames during the first computer lab session.


4.1.4 File Transfer Workflow
Automated Process (Recommended):
library(codeinput)

# Place files in submissions/[student_id]/ folders
# Run the main automation workflow (or source("main_automation_script.R"))
results <- run_automation(
  org_name = "UCL-StatSci-STAT0001-2025",
  assignment_name = "assignment-1",
  student_list_path = "student_list.csv",
  submissions_path = "submissions",
  output_dir = "output",
  reviews_per_student = 2,
  deadline = "2025-04-15",
  instructor_name = "Course Instructor"
)
Manual Process (Backup Method):
If automation fails, you can still upload files manually: 1. Create repositories individually 2. Upload files through GitHub web interface 3. Set permissions manually 4. Generate assignment lists manually


4.1.5 Managing the Review Process
Monitoring Student Engagement:
library(codeinput)

# Run daily or weekly progress checks (or source("monitor_progress_script.R"))
report <- run_progress_check(
  org_name = "UCL-StatSci-STAT0001-2025",
  assignment_name = "assignment-1",
  output_dir = "output",
  deadline = "2025-04-15",
  instructor_name = "Course Instructor"
)

# Generates in output/:
# - Repository progress summary (progress_check_[date].csv)
# - Student completion summary (student_progress_[date].csv)
# - Reviewer completion summary (reviewer_progress_[date].csv)
# - Progress plots in output/progress_reports/
# - Targeted reminder emails in output/reminders/
Facilitating Quality Reviews:

Monitor issue creation across repositories
Look for generic or unconstructive feedback
Highlight examples of excellent reviews to the class
Provide additional guidance if review quality is poor



4.1.6 Assessment Integration
Assessing Peer Review Participation:
Quantitative Measures:

Completion of required review templates (tracked via reviewer_progress_[date].csv)
Timeliness of feedback submission (last_activity in progress_check_[date].csv)
Engagement with issue discussions and pull requests

Qualitative Assessment:
# Use get_repo_issues() and get_repo_pulls() to inspect review content
# Assess based on:
# - Constructiveness of feedback
# - Specificity of observations
# - Helpful suggestions provided
# - Professional communication tone


4.1.7 Troubleshooting with Automation
Common Issues and Solutions:
GitHub Authentication or Script Failures:
Ensure your GitHub PAT has the required scopes (repo, admin:org, user) and is stored via gitcreds or .Renviron:
library(codeinput)

# Check local configuration (token, student_list.csv, submissions/)
validate_configuration()

# Test GitHub API connection and organization access
test_github_connection("UCL-StatSci-STAT0001-2025")
Error Recovery (Idempotent Re-runs):
If run_automation() is interrupted midway: 1. Review the console output for specific error messages and resolve the underlying issue. 2. Re-run run_automation(). Repository creation (create_student_repo()), file uploads (put_repo_file()), issue label creation, and reviewer branch updates (create_reviewer_branches()) are all idempotent and will safely update or skip existing resources without failing.
Student Access Problems:

Verify GitHub usernames in student_list.csv (validate_student_data() checks for missing usernames and duplicate IDs)
Confirm that students have accepted the repository invitation sent by GitHub (set_reviewer_permissions() grants collaborator access to both the submitting author and their assigned reviewers)
Use check_repo_access(repo_name, username, org_name) to verify collaborator access for a specific student

File Upload Issues:

Check file sizes (GitHub API limit: 100MB per file)
Verify file paths in submissions/[student_id]/ folders
Review console output for specific error messages

Incomplete Reviews:
library(codeinput)

# Generate targeted reminders in output/reminders/ for reviewers with pending reviews
run_progress_check(
  org_name = "UCL-StatSci-STAT0001-2025",
  assignment_name = "assignment-1",
  output_dir = "output",
  deadline = "2025-04-15",
  instructor_name = "Course Instructor"
)
Security Considerations:

Never commit your GitHub token or student data to version control
run_setup() automatically creates a .gitignore that excludes .Renviron, student_list.csv, submissions/, and output/
Regularly rotate your GitHub Personal Access Tokens and remove collaborators who no longer need access



4.1.8 Advanced Features
Customizing Review Assignments:
Use parameters in run_automation() or call assign_peer_reviewers() directly:
library(codeinput)

# Change number of reviewers per student and set a random seed for reproducibility
assignments <- assign_peer_reviewers(
  students,
  reviews_per_student = 3,
  seed = 42
)

# Or pass directly to run_automation():
results <- run_automation(
  org_name = "UCL-StatSci-STAT0001-2025",
  assignment_name = "assignment-1",
  reviews_per_student = 3,
  seed = 42
)
assign_peer_reviewers() uses a balanced circular permutation design so that every student both gives and receives exactly reviews_per_student distinct reviews, with no self-reviews or duplicate reviewer pairs.
Integration with Continuous Assessment:

Use repository activity for participation grades
Track improvement over multiple assignments
Monitor collaborative discussion quality

Scaling for Large Classes:
The automation functions handle classes up to 200+ students efficiently: - Batch processing minimizes API rate limits - Progress monitoring scales automatically - Email generation (output/email_templates/email_merge_data.csv) handles large volumes


4.1.9 Alternative Workflows
For Smaller Classes (<20 students):
Consider having all students review all submissions for maximum learning.
For Advanced Students:

Enable pull request reviews in addition to issues (using the automatically created reviewer-1, reviewer-2, … branches)
Encourage code improvement suggestions
Allow collaborative debugging sessions

For Assessment-Heavy Modules:

Use multiple rounds of peer review
Implement peer review of peer reviews (meta-review)
Create portfolio-based assessment incorporating peer feedback

title: 4  Details for Teachers
text:
4.3 Resource Requirements

4.3.1 Technical Infrastructure

GitHub Organization: Free for educational use
codeinput R Package: Open-source, installed from GitHub
R/RStudio: Free, open-source software
Computing Resources: Minimal - runs on standard academic workstations



4.3.2 Time Investment
Initial Setup (First Time):

Package installation and setup (run_setup()): 30 minutes
GitHub organization setup: 15 minutes
Student data preparation: 45 minutes
Total: ~1.5 hours

Per Assignment (Ongoing):

File organization: 15 minutes
Running run_automation(): 5 minutes
Monitoring (run_progress_check()) and reminders: 10 minutes weekly
Total: ~20 minutes + weekly monitoring



4.3.3 Support Requirements
For Students:

Provide comprehensive student guide
Offer optional GitHub tutorial sessions
Establish peer mentoring system
Create backup support during lab sessions

For Teaching Staff:

Train additional instructors on codeinput package usage
Establish backup procedures for technical failures
Document customizations and local adaptations
Plan for software updates and maintenance

title: 4  Details for Teachers
text:
4.4 Success Metrics and Expectations

4.4.1 Short-term Indicators

>90% successful repository setup
>80% completion of peer reviews within deadline
<5% technical support requests requiring instructor intervention
Positive student feedback on learning experience



4.4.2 Long-term Outcomes

Improved code quality in subsequent assignments
Increased student confidence with collaborative tools
Enhanced peer learning culture in the module
Transferable skills development for industry preparation

title: 4  Details for Teachers
text:
4.5 Emergency Procedures and Backup Plans
GitHub Service Outages:

Monitor GitHub status page
Extend deadlines if necessary
Use manual review process as fallback
Communicate clearly with students

Script Failures:

Re-run run_automation() after resolving the error (functions are idempotent)
Use validate_configuration() and test_github_connection() to diagnose issues
Revert to manual repository creation if necessary
Document issues for future improvement

Student Technical Difficulties:

Provide alternative access methods
Offer individual technical support
Consider accommodation for accessibility needs
Maintain flexible deadline policies

Remember: The codeinput package handles the complex technical setup, allowing you to focus on the pedagogical aspects of peer review and student learning outcomes. Start small with one assignment, gather feedback, and iterate based on your experience and student needs.

title: 5  Overview for Students
text: 5.1 How the Peer Review Process Works

title: 5  Overview for Students
text:
5.1.1 What Happens Behind the Scenes

Your teacher will create a private space (called a “repository” or “repo”) for your code on GitHub
Your code will be automatically moved from Moodle to this private space
Two other students will be randomly assigned to review your code
You will also be chosen to review the works of two other students
Everything is kept private - only you, your reviewers, and your teacher can see your code!



5.1.2 Your Role as a Reviewer
When you’re reviewing someone else’s code, you’ll do two things:

5.1.2.1 Part 1: Fill Out a Review Form (Required)
You are expected to answer some questions about the code you’re reviewing, such as:

Is the code easy to read and understand?
Does the code seem to work correctly?
What do you appreciate about this approach?
Do you have any suggestions for improvement?
Have you learned anything new from this code?

How to do this:

Click the link your teacher sends you to access the code (files are located in the submission/ folder)
Look for a button or link that says “Issues”
Click “New Issue”
You’ll see a Peer Review template with questions - just fill in your answers
When you’re finished, click “Submit new issue” to upload it



5.1.2.2 Part 2: Suggest Code Changes (Optional)
If you spot a bug or have an idea for improvement, you can suggest specific changes to the code on your assigned reviewer branch (reviewer-1, reviewer-2, etc.).
How to do this:

Find the code file you want to change inside the submission/ folder
Click the edit button (pencil icon)
Make your suggested changes
Write a message at the bottom, explaining what you have changed and why
Click “Propose changes” (or commit to your reviewer branch)
Click “Create pull request”
Add a description of your suggestion, and click “Create pull request” to upload it

title: 5  Overview for Students
section: 5.2 After the Review: Receiving Feedback on Your Code
text:
5.2 After the Review: Receiving Feedback on Your Code

5.2.1 Where to Find Your Reviews

Go to your private repository (your teacher will send you the link)
Click on “Issues” to see the review forms your peers filled out
Click on “Pull requests” to see any code changes they suggested



5.2.2 How to Use the Feedback

Read through all the feedback carefully
Ask questions if something isn’t clear (you can reply to issues and pull requests)
Consider implementing suggested improvements
Remember: feedback is meant to help you learn, not to criticize you personally

title: 5  Overview for Students
text:
5.3 Tips
The rOpenSci initiative has some great resources for code peer review. Below are some helpful tips.

5.3.1 Common GitHub Terms Explained

Repository (Repo): Your private folder containing your code
Issue: A place to discuss problems, ask questions, or give feedback
Pull Request: A suggested change to the code
Branch: Different versions of your code (don’t worry about this too much for now)
Commit: Saving changes to your code



5.3.2 Writing Good Reviews

Be kind and constructive: Instead of “This is wrong,” try “Have you considered trying this approach?”
Be specific: Point out exactly what you’re referring to
Highlight good things too: If someone did something clever, tell them!
Ask questions: “Why did you choose this method?” can lead to good discussions



5.3.3 When You’re Stuck

Don’t panic! GitHub can seem overwhelming at first
Ask your teacher or classmates for help
Most buttons are safe to click - you won’t break anything
Remember that everyone is learning



5.3.4 Making the Most of Feedback

Don’t take criticism personally - it’s about the code, not you
Try to understand why reviewers made their suggestions
Feel free to ask follow-up questions
Use the feedback to improve your next assignment

title: 5  Overview for Students
text:
5.4 Getting Help
If you get stuck:

Ask a classmate
Ask your teacher during lab sessions or through the Moodle forum
Check the GitHub help documentation
Remember: everyone finds GitHub confusing at first!

Remember: The goal isn’t to become a GitHub expert overnight, but to learn from each other and improve your coding skills together!

title: 6  Set-up for Students
text:
6.0.1 Step 1: Create Your GitHub Account
If you already have a GitHub account under another email address and want to use it for the code review, then please go to the next section. Otherwise:

Go to github.com

Click “Sign up”

Choose a username (tip: it’s recommended to use something professional, as you might later use this account for job applications!)

Use your UCL email address

Create a strong password

Verify your email when GitHub sends you a message



6.0.2 Step 2: Upload Your Assignment to Moodle

Submit your code assignment to Moodle as you normally would

Also include your GitHub username in your submission, unless your teacher has other specific requests (in that case, follow their instructions).

title: 7  FAQs
text: 7.1 For Students:

title: 7  FAQs
text:
How many reviews should I do, and who are going to review my work?


Reviews are assigned randomly; the exact number is defined by the course. Please follow the lecturer’s latest announcements for any special arrangements.


I can’t open the repo or didn’t receive an invite. What should I do?


First, you should confirm that you have been enrolled on Moodle and added to the course’s GitHub organisation. If you are still unable to access the repo, please provide your name, student ID, and GitHub username/email, to the lecturer or teaching team.


Why use GitHub for peer review?


GitHub provides private repositories, standardised issue templates, and an auditable history. This makes it easier to allocate tasks, keep reviewing evidence, and follow up. Becoming familiar with GitHub is also helpful for your future study and work.


Can I comment on a single line or a specific code snippet?


Yes. In the file view, click the line number to get a URL with an anchor like #L42 or #L10-L20; paste that link into the Issue to point precisely. Press the y key on the file page to turn it into a permalink so it stays stable after edits. You can also paste a small snippet in the comment and briefly explain the context and suggestion.


Do I need to run someone else’s code in my local environment?


Usually no——running untrusted code can be risky. If the template or course requires execution, use a safe, isolated environment (e.g., virtual environment or container), and follow the notes and sample data provided by the course. If you prefer not to run the code locally, you can use GitHub Codespaces in the browser. Always remember to follow safety guidance of your courses and avoid running suspicious scripts.


I can’t see other students’ repos. Is that expected?


Yes. Repos are private by default and visible only to the author, assigned reviewers, and the teaching team.

title: 7  FAQs
text:
7.2 For Lecturer:

Can we start without having every student’s GitHub username?


Yes. We can directly invite students to the organisation or specific repos by email. They can accept with a GitHub account that has been verified, or sign up during acceptance.


Students report “no access” or can’t open their repo, what should we check first?


Confirm that their GitHub username in student_list.csv is accurate and that they have accepted the repository invitation sent by GitHub (set_reviewer_permissions() grants collaborator access to both the submitting student and their assigned reviewers). You can verify collaborator status at any time using check_repo_access(repo_name, username, org_name).


How do we control how many reviews each student gives or each submission receives?


Use the reviews_per_student parameter in run_automation() (or assign_peer_reviewers()), which assigns a balanced circular permutation so each student both gives and receives reviews_per_student distinct reviews. Before full rollout, a dry-run on a small roster is recommended to validate workload and connectivity. It is also recommended to announce this information to all students via email or on the Moodle page.


Do we need anonymous peer review on GitHub?


By default, it is not anonymous because usernames are visible. If anonymity is required, use pseudonymous accounts or collect reviews via a separate form and post summaries back to the repo.


After the deadline students keep pushing changes, what version is graded?


By default, grading is based on the version at the stated deadline. Later changes may remain for students to further learning, but they should not affect grading unless your course policy says otherwise.


How do we monitor completion and chase late reviewers?


Run run_progress_check(), which queries Issues and Pull Requests across all student repositories, generates progress_check_[date].csv, student_progress_[date].csv, and reviewer_progress_[date].csv in output/, saves progress visualizations in output/progress_reports/, and creates targeted reminder emails in output/reminders/ for reviewers with incomplete reviews.


Some students withdrew or never accepted invites, how do we fix lopsided assignments?


You should mark those students inactive and reassign only the edges touching them. Keep all other assignments intact to minimise churn.


What naming and visibility scheme is recommended?


By default, run_automation() creates private repositories using the pattern student-{student_id}-{assignment_name} (e.g., student-12345-assignment-1). Personalized repository and reviewer branch links are automatically included in output/student_repo_links.csv and output/email_templates/.
